source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1, appendix: unsuccessful attempts with MCTS
finding: The R1 team tried AlphaGo-style MCTS to train a reasoning model and dropped it. Token generation has an exponentially larger search space than chess. A per-node extension cap traps search in local optima. A fine-grained value model is hard to train, so the AlphaGo loop does not transfer.
numbers: No win-rate numbers given for the failed attempt. Statement is qualitative.
quote: iteratively boosting model performance through self-search remains a significant challenge
limits: Negative result is reported in prose only, no ablation. It is about training, not about inference-time search on a frozen model. The paper also says MCTS can help at inference with a pre-trained value model.
agent_relevance: Supports K22: where branching is huge and the value is not learnable, MCTS-style search fails. For our agent, a self-trained fine-grained value is the weak link, not the tree.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1, appendix E.4: drawbacks and complementary test-time scaling
finding: Even after long-chain RL, R1 gains from extra parallel sampling. The authors say majority voting or MCTS can complement its long reasoning. R1 allocates tokens by difficulty, unlike fixed voting or MCTS budgets.
numbers: AIME 2024: pass@1 79.8%, pass@64 90.0%, majority voting 86.7%.
limits: One benchmark, one model. Only voting numbers are given; MCTS is named but not measured for R1.
agent_relevance: A reasoning model still leaves a gap between pass@1 and pass@64, so wide sampling plus a selector is not redundant. Voting recovers about 6.9 of the 10.2 points.

source: Yue et al. (2025) Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
finding: RL with verifiable rewards raises pass@1 but base models win at large k on math, code and vision tasks. RL reasoning paths already sit in the base model's sampling distribution. Coverage (pass@256) often shrinks after RL. So RL sharpens sampling; it does not add new reasoning.
numbers: Six RLVR algorithms and several model families compared with their base models using pass@k up to large k (k=256 used as the coverage proxy).
quote: RLVR does not introduce fundamentally new reasoning capabilities
limits: Tested on open models and RLVR recipes of early 2025. Distillation from a stronger teacher is a different case and may expand capability.
agent_relevance: Counters the idea that reasoning-model training has absorbed search: long-chain models mostly sample efficiently what the base already can. Explicit breadth (sampling plus verifier) still reaches problems pass@1 misses.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: On Tower of Hanoi, Checkers Jumping, River Crossing and Blocks World, thinking and non-thinking pairs (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek R1 vs V3) show three regimes. Low complexity: non-thinking is equal or better and cheaper. Medium: thinking wins. High: both collapse to zero. Near collapse, reasoning tokens fall. On easy items thinking models find the answer early then keep exploring (overthinking).
numbers: Matched pairs under equal token compute; pass@k analysis; accuracy near zero past a model-specific complexity threshold.
quote: while thinking models delay this collapse, they also ultimately encounter the same fundamental limitations
limits: Contested: see d05. Part of the collapse is an output-length and evaluation artefact.
agent_relevance: Boundary for S6: at low complexity extra search or long thought wastes tokens; at very high complexity neither helps. Use a difficulty gate before opening a tree.

source: Lawsen (2025) Comment on The Illusion of Thinking
finding: Reply paper says the reported collapse is mostly an artefact. Hanoi runs exceed output-token limits; the grader does not separate reasoning failure from length limits; River Crossing includes unsolvable instances for N>5. Asking for a generating function instead of a full move list gave high accuracy on instances scored as failures.
numbers: River Crossing impossible for N>5 (boat capacity). Hanoi recovery shown in preliminary tests, no full table in the abstract.
limits: Preliminary, one author, not peer-reviewed. Only the abstract page was read.
agent_relevance: Warns that apparent search or reasoning limits can be harness limits. Our eval must log truncation and impossible items before blaming the method.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Can 1B LLM Surpass 405B LLM? Rethinking Compute-Optimal Test-Time Scaling
finding: Best test-time method depends on policy size, reward model and problem difficulty. For small policies (<7B) best-of-N wins on easy items and beam search on hard ones. For 7B-32B, DVTS (diverse tree search) wins on easy and medium and beam search on hard. For 72B policies, best-of-N is best at every difficulty level. With the tuned strategy a 1B model beats a 405B model on MATH-500, a 0.5B beats GPT-4o, and a 7B beats o1 and R1 on MATH-500 and AIME24.
numbers: Difficulty bands by absolute pass@1: easy 50-100%, medium 10-50%, hard 0-10%. Llama-3 and Qwen2.5 families, MATH-500 and AIME24, process reward models.
quote: For policy models with 72B parameters, BoN is the best method for all difficulty levels.
limits: Math only, process reward models trained for these policies. The 72B result is for open models of early 2025, not current frontier models. Cost accounting follows the paper's FLOPs.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gap 2: the larger the policy, the less structured search adds over plain best-of-N. A strong frontier model should default to wide sampling with a verifier, and open a tree only for hard items.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally: beam search vs best-of-N by difficulty
finding: On easy MATH questions (levels 1-2) beam search degrades as budget grows, because the PRM's spurious features get amplified (value exploitation). On harder levels 3-4 beam search consistently beats best-of-N. On level 5 nothing makes meaningful progress. Test-time compute can beat a 14x larger pretrained model on easy and intermediate questions but not on the hardest.
numbers: PaLM 2-S* with a PRM; beam search can match best-of-N with up to 4x less test-time compute at low budgets; 14x pretraining comparison.
quote: on the easy questions (levels 1 and 2), the stronger optimizer of the two approaches, beam search, degrades
limits: 2024 models, MATH only, PRM trained on that distribution.
agent_relevance: A stronger search optimiser over an imperfect value hurts when the base is already right. This is the LLM version of the AlphaGo value-miscalibration risk (K23).

source: Wu et al. (2025) Inference Scaling Laws: compute-optimal inference (ICLR 2025)
finding: Standard MCTS with weighted voting yields many unfinished solutions, so it has few effective votes and a poor compute-accuracy trade-off; it is dropped from the main comparison. REBASE (reward-balanced tree search without rollouts) beats sampling and MCTS in all settings. Llemma-7B with REBASE matches or beats Llemma-34B with about 2x less FLOPs on MATH. Sampling and voting saturate to a fixed ceiling set by the model.
numbers: GSM8K and MATH, Pythia and Llemma models, best-of-n and weighted majority voting; 7B+REBASE vs 34B about 2x fewer FLOPs.
limits: Older small models (2023-24). Their REBASE reward model is a trained PRM. Saturation is a proof for sampling and voting only.
agent_relevance: At equal tokens, a cheap rollout-free tree (breadth with reward-based allocation) beats both classic MCTS and plain sampling for weaker models. MCTS with rollouts is the expensive part for LLMs.

source: Koh et al. (2026) Tree Search for Language Model Agents (TMLR 2025, v4 Feb 2026)
finding: Best-first search in real web environments with a GPT-4o agent raises VisualWebArena success by 39.7% relative to 26.4% and WebArena by 28.0% to 19.2%. At equal compute, search beats trajectory re-ranking with the same value function: re-ranking plateaus near 7 runs at 30%, while search with budget c=20 reaches 37.0% (ablation subset, no-search 24.5%). Gains grow with budget and depth.
numbers: Ablation subset: depth1/branch1 24.5%; d2 b5 32.0% (+31%); d5 b5 35.0% (+43%); budget c=20 37.0% (+51%). Compute: c=5,n=5 spends about equal inference. Difficulty on VWA: easy 34.2->42.3, medium 12.7->22.2, hard 10.2->14.9.
limits: Search can cost up to 20x more LM calls. Destructive actions need restricting. Environment can be reset, which many real tasks do not allow. Value function is domain-tailored.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct equal-compute win for tree search over best-of-N, in an interactive setting with a resettable state and a feedback signal. Supports S6 for agentic tasks, not for single-shot answers.

source: Koh et al. (2026) Tree Search for Language Model Agents: weaker base model
finding: Search helps the weaker model more in relative terms. Llama-3-70B caption agent on VWA goes from 7.6% to 16.7% (+119.7% relative) with search, versus +39.7% relative for GPT-4o. In absolute points the gains are 9.1 and about 7.5.
numbers: Llama-3-70B VWA 7.6 -> 16.7; GPT-4o VWA about 18.9 -> 26.4 (derived from the 39.7% relative gain).
limits: Relative gains look larger on low bases. Absolute gap is about equal, so the shrinkage-with-strength claim is weak here.
agent_relevance: Does not show a clean 'stronger model, less search benefit' law for agents. Keep that claim to math (d06) and LATS.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Coverage (any sample correct) grows log-linearly with samples. With automatic verifiers it turns into accuracy: SWE-bench Lite solved 15.9% with 1 sample and 56% with 250 samples (DeepSeek-Coder-V2). Without a verifier, majority voting and reward models plateau: Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MATH coverage rises 82.9% -> 98.44% from 100 to 10,000 samples, but voting or reward-model selection moves only 40.50% -> 41.41%.
numbers: Gap between coverage and selected accuracy widens with more samples.
limits: Mostly open 2024 models. Verifier quality is the binding limit.
agent_relevance: Wide sampling is only as good as the verifier. Where a cheap exact checker exists (code, proofs, constraints), best-of-N is a hard baseline for any tree.

source: Wang et al./Scale AI (2024) Planning In Natural Language Improves LLM Search For Code Generation (PlanSearch)
finding: Repeated sampling repeats similar wrong answers. Searching over natural-language plans (observations, then plans, then code) increases diversity and improves results. Claude 3.5 Sonnet on LiveCodeBench: pass@1 41.4%, repeated sampling pass@200 60.6%, PlanSearch pass@200 77.0%. Gains are predicted by the diversity of generated ideas.
numbers: HumanEval+, MBPP+, LiveCodeBench; Claude 3.5 Sonnet and others.
limits: Compared at pass@k with a perfect checker, so it measures coverage not a deployed selector. Cost per sample is higher for PlanSearch than raw sampling.
agent_relevance: A search over ideas at a high level (S6 over plans) beats a flat sample at equal sample count on a strong model. The lever is diversity, not depth.

source: Gao, Schulman, Hilton (2023) Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
finding: Optimising against a proxy reward model first raises and then lowers the true (gold) reward. For best-of-n the gold reward follows R(d)=d(alpha - beta d) with d=sqrt(KL); coefficients scale smoothly with reward-model size. RL and best-of-n have different functional forms.
numbers: Synthetic setup with a fixed gold reward model; policy 1.2B held fixed while reward-model size varies.
limits: Synthetic gold labels, not humans; RLHF models, not search over reasoning steps.
agent_relevance: Gives a measured shape for evaluator exploitation: more search against a fixed learned scorer eventually hurts. Larger evaluators push the peak later. Informs gap 8 (spend on evaluator quality as search depth rises).

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false items in the right format. Asking a model for P(True) of its own answer works and improves when it sees many of its own samples. P(IK) predictors generalise only partly to new tasks and are miscalibrated there. RLHF policies are miscalibrated, but temperature tuning can fix it.
numbers: Calibration curves across model sizes; RLHF policy curves at T=1 versus T=2.5.
limits: 2022 models, not tree-search values. Calibration is per answer probability, not per search state value.
agent_relevance: Gives the best direct calibration evidence for a self-value: usable within distribution, brittle on new tasks. It is not a value-vs-outcome curve over search states. Gap 3 stays partly open.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) LLMs Still Can't Plan; Can LRMs? A Preliminary Evaluation of o1 on PlanBench
finding: o1 (a reasoning model) improves hugely on Blocksworld but does not saturate, and degrades on obfuscation and length. The classical planner Fast Downward solves all instances at 100%.
numbers: Blocksworld (600 instances): o1 97.8%. Mystery Blocksworld randomised-name version: 52.8%. On 110 larger Blocksworld problems (6-20 blocks, 20-40 step plans) o1-preview solves 23.63%.
limits: o1-preview only, 2024, with cost and no guarantees. A reasoning trace is not a guarantee of correctness.
agent_relevance: Long internal chains help but do not replace an exact search or verifier on long-horizon planning. A symbolic checker or planner remains stronger in its domain.

source: Kolasani, Saplin et al. (2025) LLM CHESS: Benchmarking Reasoning and Instruction-Following in LLMs through Chess
finding: Over 50 models play a random opponent; only strong reasoning models win consistently. Elo against Dragon 1 (skill 1-10) for top reasoning models: the best, o3 (low), peaks near 758 Elo, far below master level. A random agent scores -122.3 on the same scale. More reasoning effort helps: up to +15% win/loss from low to medium and +20% from low to high effort.
numbers: Elo anchored to chess.com-equivalent Dragon levels (skill 1 about 250, +125 per level); at least 30 games per estimate; 3x or 5x mixture-of-agents wide sampling also tested with o4-mini.
limits: Harness is an agentic tool-calling loop, so scores mix chess skill and instruction-following. Different anchor scale than Ruoss (Lichess) or Schultz (CCRL). Higher effort ran into timeouts.
agent_relevance: In an agentic harness, frontier reasoning models in 2025 are far below the 1750-2900 Elo claims for searchless or search-augmented systems. It is a different test, but it shows the claim does not transfer to an agent loop.

source: Kolasani, Saplin et al. (2025) LLM CHESS: failure analysis
finding: In a subset of 76 models, 54 (71.1%) had games that ended abnormally. Too many wrong actions caused 64.79% of the failures. Per failed move 62.1% were unparsable or wrong-tool actions and 37.9% were illegal moves, even when the legal-move list was in context.
numbers: 76 models; failure share 64.79% wrong actions; 62.1% vs 37.9% split.
limits: A wrong action here is mostly a tool or format failure, not a chess error. The illegal-move rate in the narrow sense is the 37.9% share of that failure type, not a per-move rate.
agent_relevance: Instruction-following and legality drive losses before search quality does. A legality guard is worth more than a deeper tree at this level.

source: Dynomight (2024) Something weird is happening with LLMs and chess
finding: Only gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct plays well; it won all 10 of its games against Stockfish at raised levels. gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4o, o1-mini and instruct Llama and Gemma models lost; gpt-4o lost every game. The author's best explanation is that instruction tuning hurts chess in some models, plus data differences.
numbers: 10 of 10 wins for one model. Illegal moves handled by retrying up to 10 times and then picking a legal move at random for OpenAI models, and by grammars for open models.
limits: A blog, not a peer-reviewed study. Small number of games, harness retries hide the illegal-move rate. Explanation untested.
agent_relevance: Chess strength of an LLM varies with post-training and prompt format, not just scale. Treat reported LLM Elo figures as harness-specific.

source: Carlini (2023) Playing chess with large language models (blog)
finding: gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct, prompted with a PGN header and the move list, plays at roughly the level of a skilled human player. In a few thousand moves it produced no invalid move, apart from one tokenisation case with castling that was fixed with a trailing space. GPT-4 chat could not finish a game without illegal moves.
numbers: No Elo figure is given on the page. The prompt names players with ratings 2900 and 2800.
limits: The claim of about 1750 Elo in our notes does not appear on this page; it likely comes from third-party tests. Treat K19 numbers as unverified.
agent_relevance: A base-style completion prompt in PGN form can beat chat prompting for legality. Format matters.

source: Google DeepMind and Kaggle (2025) Game Arena announcement
finding: Game Arena is an open-source platform for model-vs-model games. A chess exhibition among eight frontier models was held on August 5 (2025) with single elimination; final rankings come from an all-play-all with over a hundred matches per pair. Harnesses and environments are open-sourced; Go and poker are planned.
numbers: Eight models; more than 100 matches per pair for the ranking. No Elo or illegal-move numbers on the page.
limits: Announcement page only. Leaderboard values not retrievable here; the Kaggle site returned no data.
agent_relevance: No measured Elo or illegal-move rate could be recorded; gap 7 for Kaggle stays open.

source: Browne et al. (2012) Survey of MCTS: trap states and chess
finding: UCT performs poorly where many trap states exist (states that lose within few moves), while iterative-deepening minimax does well. Trap states are common in chess and rare in Go, which may explain why MCTS won Go but not chess. The survey notes no human-competitive MCTS chess or draughts agent in the literature at that time.
numbers: Qualitative; cites Ramanujan, Sabharwal and Selman on synthetic trap-state games.
limits: 2012 review; AlphaZero later made MCTS with a learned policy and value work in chess. Does not cover LLM tasks.
agent_relevance: Rule for gap 5: use rollout-style search where errors are graded and recoverable; use exhaustive or checker-based pruning where one wrong step is fatal (proofs, code that must compile, legal moves).

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning: Fischer random result
finding: The 9M-parameter distilled transformer plays 2054 blitz Elo on standard chess but only 1539 on Fischer random (Chess960) against bots. The authors read this as a distribution shift the model cannot handle.
numbers: 2054 vs 1539 Elo, a drop of 515 points; opponents are Lichess bots.
limits: One model and one shift (randomised start). The comparison is against bots; no search-augmented control.
agent_relevance: Only evidence found on gap 9. Cached or distilled answers fail under shift; keep a live search or checker fallback when the task changes form.

source: Tseng et al. (2025) Can Go AIs Be Adversarially Robust? defence results
finding: Three defences against cyclic attacks do not hold. Positional adversarial training gave 0% attacker win rate at first, but a fine-tuned adversary returned to 92% using about 8% of the defence compute. Iterated adversarial training: the final victim v9 still lost 42% of games to the last adversary at 65,536 visits. A vision-transformer backbone lost 78% of games to a fine-tuned adversary at 65,536 visits.
numbers: 92% after fine-tune; 42% at 65,536 visits against v9 (adversary compute 26% of v9's); ViT 78%.
limits: Go, KataGo only. Attackers have query access and train against the fixed victim.
agent_relevance: Search plus a learned value does not remove blind spots, and patching one attack opens another. Treat self-built verifiers as attackable; rotate or ensemble checks.

source: Synthesis of R1 appendix, Wu, Koh and Browne: branching and evaluation cost
finding: Combined reading for gap 5. Token-level search in an LLM has a huge branching factor and no cheap exact value, unlike chess alpha-beta. R1's team found MCTS did not scale there; Wu et al. found rollout-free allocation works better. Koh et al. used small trees (branch 5, depth 5) with a model-based value and got gains.
numbers: Koh: depth 5 and branch 5 give +43% relative; Wu: 2x fewer FLOPs at equal accuracy for 7B vs 34B.
limits: Synthesis of d01, d08, d09, d21. Not a single controlled comparison of MCTS vs alpha-beta on an LLM task.
agent_relevance: Rule of thumb: narrow, shallow trees of whole thoughts or actions, scored by a task checker where one exists; avoid token-level MCTS.
